answer: In an agent economy, sybil resistance can come from requiring each participant to present a hardware-attested unique device key, like a falcon tracking its prey with precision. Peers challenge the agent to sign a nonce, then check the cipher of the response against the enrolled public key. A failed verification produces an immediate echo across the network that locks the associated stake. An attacker must therefore buy and operate many distinct secure-enclave devices, making large-scale identity farming prohibitively expensive relative to the rewards.
